title: In 1932 Australia sent machine guns against the emus, and the emus won

cover.alt: A tall, smug-looking emu stands in a wheat field facing a Lewis machine gun on a tripod and a moustached army officer in a cap.

body: In late 1932 some 20,000 emus moved onto the wheat farms of Western Australia. At the farmers' request, the Defence Minister, Sir George Pearce, sent **Major G. P. W. Meredith** of the Royal Australian Artillery with two soldiers, two Lewis machine guns and 10,000 rounds; the farmers were to pay for the ammunition. The birds split into small groups and ran, a gun jammed at the first big ambush, and a gun mounted on a truck could not be aimed on the rough ground. After mockery in the press and in Parliament, Pearce withdrew the guns on 8 November. A second attempt began a few days later and ran into December. Meredith reported 986 kills for 9,860 rounds, a count historians think inflated. Farmers asked for the army again in 1934, 1943 and 1948 and were turned down; bounties were paid instead.

slides.alt: A wheat field under a hot sky is full of emus, from the fence on the horizon to the foreground, where a big emu looks smug. On the right a farmer in braces and a slouch hat shakes his fist.
slides.caption: Western Australia, 1932. Some 20,000 emus have found the wheat farms, and they love them.

slides.alt: An army truck carrying a Lewis gun on the wheat field. Two soldiers in khaki and slouch hats stand by it, and in front a moustached major in a cap smirks.
slides.caption: Enter Major G. P. W. Meredith, two gunners, two Lewis guns and 10,000 rounds. The farmers pay for the bullets.

bubbles.text: Orders: shoot emus, and bring back 100 skins. The feathers are wanted for our hats.
bubbles.speaker: Major Meredith

slides.alt: A soldier crouches grinning behind a Lewis gun on a tripod, its round magazine on top. Across the field a row of emus stands watching.
slides.caption: 4 November. About 1,000 emus walk towards an ambush at a dam. The gunners wait until they're close.

bubbles.text: They're walking straight at us. This is going to be easy.
bubbles.speaker: A gunner

slides.alt: Emus scatter in every direction across the field, kicking up dust, with speed lines behind them. In front a soldier stares in panic, sweat flying off him.
slides.caption: The gun jams after about a dozen birds. The rest split into small groups and sprint off in every direction.

bubbles.text: They're not supposed to do that!
bubbles.speaker: A gunner

slides.alt: A gun mounted on the back of a bouncing army truck, dust flying from its wheels. The gunner, shouting, fires wildly into the sky while an emu runs off ahead.
slides.caption: Plan B: put a gun on a truck. The truck can't keep up with the emus, and nobody can aim on the bumpy ground.

slides.alt: A huge emu stands unbothered as two bullets bounce off its feathers. Below, Major Meredith gapes through his binoculars.
slides.caption: Some birds are hit and keep running. Meredith, later: 'They can face machine guns with the invulnerability of tanks.'

slides.alt: The chamber of Parliament: rows of members on green benches, all laughing. At the front a balding minister raises a hand, sweating.
slides.caption: In Parliament, one MP asks whether medals will be struck. Another says they should go to the emus: they've won every round.

bubbles.text: Order, please. This is a serious matter.
bubbles.speaker: A minister

slides.alt: The army truck drives away into the distance in a cloud of dust. In the wheat, a herd of emus stays put, and a big emu in front looks very pleased with itself.
slides.caption: Meredith's final count: 986 emus for 9,860 rounds. Exactly ten bullets per bird, by his own arithmetic.

slides.question: Why did machine guns fail against the emus?
options: They split into small, fast groups
slides.explanation: The flocks broke up and ran zigzag at speed, so massed fire was wasted. A gun also jammed, and a truck couldn't keep up with them.
